title: Tide and Garden Again
premise: Silas Underhill has spent ten years writing letters to a stranger she's never met — a correspondence that began as a grief ritual after her grandfather's death and became the truest relationship of her life. When the letters suddenly stop, she assumes the worst, until a new neighbor arrives in the coastal village of Brackenlow: a woman named Wren, who is fleeing a wrongful conviction and the machinery that ruined her, and who turns out to be the person on the other end of every letter. As Wren seeks justice outside a legal system that failed her, Silas must finally speak the sentence she has rehearsed for a decade — that she loves her — before Wren is forced to run again. In the end, they expose the real culprit together, and Silas learns that second chances aren't about timing; they're about choosing to stay.
about_author: Jude Thornbury is a former maritime archivist who spent years cataloguing lighthouse logs along the northern coast before turning to fiction full-time. They write slow-burn romances about people who find home in unlikely places, usually near water.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Ten years of letters to 'W' have ended abruptly; the final reply arrived months ago and nothing since. Silas tends the decommissioned lighthouse garden her grandfather kept, rereading old letters, telling herself she isn't waiting. Emotional beat: quiet dread disguised as routine.

chapters.title: A Moving Van in November
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. A new tenant takes the cottage next door: a guarded woman named Wren who flinches at cameras and asks odd questions about mail delivery. Silas offers cuttings from the garden; Wren declines but watches her too long. Emotional beat: curiosity sparking against instinctive wariness.

chapters.title: What the Tide Brought Back
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren unpacks boxes containing evidence no court would touch — ledger pages proving her former employer framed her for embezzlement. She recognizes Silas immediately from the return address on a decade of letters and panics: the one person who knows her handwriting lives thirty feet away. Emotional beat: terror braided with longing.

chapters.title: Salt on Every Page
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Sorting her grandfather's papers, Silas finds a letter she never sent — the confession she wrote at nineteen and never mailed. She burns it in the garden fire pit while Wren watches from her window. Emotional beat: grief for the girl who couldn't speak.

chapters.title: Neighbors, Technically
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. A village storm knocks out power; Silas brings candles, Wren can't refuse hospitality twice. They talk about everything except themselves. Wren almost slips about the letters; Silas notices Wren's phrasing echoes 'W's' exactly. Emotional beat: intimacy arriving sideways.

chapters.title: The Sentence Rehearsed
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Flashback chapter: how the correspondence began — a grief-stricken letter slipped into a library book, answered by a stranger. We see young Silas rehearsing 'I love you' into a tape recorder and deleting it. Present-day Silas drafts the sentence again and doesn't send it. Emotional beat: tenderness sharpened by regret.

chapters.title: Someone Is Asking Questions
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A private investigator hired by her old employer appears in Brackenlow, photographing the harbor. Wren realizes staying endangers everyone near her — including Silas, whose name is already in his notes. Emotional beat: protective panic hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Garden Logic
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas teaches Wren to graft roses — her grandfather's method — and Wren, hands in the dirt, nearly tells the truth. Instead she says, 'What would you do if someone you trusted turned out to be a lie?' Silas answers honestly: 'I'd want to know why before I decided what they were.' Emotional beat: forgiveness offered in advance, unclaimed.

chapters.title: Confession by Firelight
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Wren breaks: she shows Silas the letters she wrote, all ten years of them, and the ledger pages. Silas's world tilts — the stranger she loved was next door all along, and she never knew. Anger, relief, and devastation collide. Emotional beat: the truth landing like a wave.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Timing
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas rages — not at the deception but at herself, for loving an abstraction while the real person stood within reach. She walks the tideline all night. Wren packs a bag, assuming she's lost her. Emotional beat: heartbreak on both sides of one wall.

chapters.title: The Investigator's Offer
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The PI corners Wren: drop the ledger, leave town, or he'll leak her location to people who want her silenced permanently. He mentions Silas by name. Wren agrees to leave — but first she'll copy the ledger and hide it where only Silas could find it. Emotional beat: sacrifice disguised as surrender.

chapters.title: Empty Cottage
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas returns to find Wren gone and a single letter on the doorstep — Wren's goodbye, containing the sentence Silas has waited a decade to hear, given now when it's too late to answer. Silas reads it eleven times. Emotional beat: devastating reciprocity.

chapters.title: What Grandfather Knew
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Digging through lighthouse logs for distraction, Silas discovers her grandfather once sheltered a fugitive in 1974 and hid evidence in the keeper's registry — proof that justice here has always lived outside the courthouse. She understands exactly where Wren would hide the ledger copy. Emotional beat: inheritance of courage.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Registry
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas finds the hidden ledger duplicate sealed in the old lamp room, plus Wren's contingency note: 'If you're reading this, you chose to look. That's the whole answer.' Silas stops grieving and starts planning. Emotional beat: resolve igniting.

chapters.title: An Unlikely Alliance
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas recruits the village postmistress, a retired journalist, and the pub landlord — people the law never protected either. They map the employer's network using the ledger. The PI is spotted watching the cottage again. Emotional beat: a small town becoming a fortress.

chapters.title: Bait
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Silas lets the PI 'discover' that Wren kept copies, forcing his employers to move before Wren can be found — buying time but painting a target on Silas. Wren, hiding two towns over, sees the news and realizes what Silas has done. Emotional beat: love expressed as recklessness.

chapters.title: Running Toward
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren abandons safety and comes back, breaking her own rule for the first time in ten years. She reaches Brackenlow during a gale just as the PI's employers arrive to search the lighthouse. Emotional beat: fear outrun by devotion.

chapters.title: The Lamp Room
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Climax: confrontation in the lighthouse during the storm. The PI demands the ledger; Silas stalls; Wren arrives; the retired journalist has been broadcasting the whole encounter live to a national audience. The employers' fixer backs down under public exposure. The PI is arrested on unrelated warrants. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into triumph.

chapters.title: Aftermath and Apples
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Days later: the employer is formally investigated, journalists circle, and Wren's conviction looks likely to collapse. But fame frightens Wren more than flight ever did. Silas plants an apple tree with her — her grandfather's last unopened seed packet. Emotional beat: fragile peace taking root.

chapters.title: The Sentence Spoken
chapters.summary: Both POVs. On the lighthouse gallery at dawn, Silas finally says the sentence she rehearsed for a decade — not 'I love you' as written at nineteen, but its grown-up version: 'I choose you, out loud, on purpose, with timing be damned.' Wren answers with the letter she wrote at seventeen and never had the courage to mean until now. Emotional beat: ten years resolving into one spoken moment.

chapters.title: Belonging
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren signs a lease, then something bigger: her name cleared, she donates the ledger archive to the village historical society beside her grandfather-era counterpart. She writes one last letter and hand-delivers it across the garden wall. Emotional beat: exile ending.

chapters.title: Tide and Garden Again
chapters.summary: Silas's POV, epilogue. One year later: the apple tree blossoms, Silas's novel about a lighthouse keeper and a fugitive is finished, and the two of them keep a shared journal passed over the fence — no longer out of necessity but ritual. Final line mirrors the first letter ever sent. Emotional beat: full-circle belonging.
